claims.text: The native eutectic high-entropy alloy contains mechanically softer, wear-sensitive regions and harder regions.
The softer phase is less corrosion-resistant, while the harder phase is more corrosion-resistant.
Mechanical wear preferentially removes the protective passive or oxide film from the softer phase.
Removal of the protective film locally exposes the softer phase to the corrosive environment and increases its anodic susceptibility.
A galvanic potential difference between the constituent phases accelerates localized corrosion of the exposed phase.
Localized corrosion further destabilizes the passive film and weakens interphase regions.
Corrosion-induced weakening promotes additional wear, forming a self-reinforcing tribocorrosion feedback loop.
Distinct phases can have different mechanical roles during wear, including a ductile FCC phase that supports a hard sigma phase and forms a wear-reducing oxide layer.
A hard sigma phase can restrict crack generation and propagation and contribute to improved anti-wear behavior.
Differential phase properties produce dissimilar passive-film stability and mediate localized galvanic coupling under wear.
Processing can generate a reduced-heterogeneity or homogenized comparison microstructure while keeping alloy composition identical.
Relative to the homogenized baseline, the native heterogeneous alloy will have a significantly higher overall degradation rate.
Relative to the baseline, the native heterogeneous alloy will exhibit more aggressive wear because its soft phase undergoes rapid protective-film removal.
Relative to the baseline, the native heterogeneous alloy will exhibit a higher corrosion rate or corrosion current density because of localized galvanic effects.
The homogenized baseline will show lower, nearly additive wear and corrosion responses without positive feedback.
The proposed feedback mechanism applies above approximately 600 °C in a NaCl-containing corrosive medium when distinct soft and hard phases are present.
Elevated temperature enhances both chemical reactivity and mechanical wear.
The cited prior studies support a link between microstructural heterogeneity, passive-film stability, and localized corrosion.

Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in total degradation and corresponding wear and corrosion metrics in the heterogeneous sample would falsify the proposed heterogeneity-driven feedback mechanism.
